evidence.text_en:
Build your own heat pump in an honest practical test: two years testing

Important notice upfront. Of course, the electricity must be prepared or connected by an electrician. Safety always comes first when connecting to the grid. In this video I take you along on my big adventure installing an air-water heat pump myself. I show you my device and my system in the garden and tell you honestly and unvarnished how I implemented the entire project on my own, what hurdles there were, and how my system works after now twenty years of wood stove experience. To avoid any trouble, I've taped over the logo and model designation on the heat pump for the video. Here's what to expect in the video. First. The backstory and my motivation. I tell you why after installing my solar panels, which I show you in the video, I absolutely wanted a heat pump and why a simple immersion heater in a water tank was not an option for me. My solar system has a proud ten kilowatts peak capacity. Second. The rock-solid foundation. I tell you how I saved myself from pouring a concrete slab. You learn how I dug out the earth, packed it with stones and water, and placed an old thick concrete block with twenty centimetres overhang on top. Third. The pipes and insulation. Why I chose thick, weatherproof rubber insulation and flexible white PE pipes. I also tell you how I laid the lines ten metres through under the floorboards to the water tank. Fourth. The honest noise check. I show you the heat pump outside in the garden and tell you how loud the device really is and why the control panel directly on my bedroom wall doesn't disturb my sleep at night at all. Fifth. The technology and safety components. I explain why the passive pressure of my old system wasn't enough for the heat pump. You learn all about installing the additional pump, the check valve, the strainer, the dirt separator and the filter. Sixth. Why the self-installation is legal. I explain why the factory-sealed monoblock system of the heat pump means that you as a DIYer can legally lay the pipes yourself. Seventh. The weak points of the cheap heat pump. I haven't opened the device for the video, but I tell you exactly what's hidden inside. We talk about the missing partition wall between the heat chamber and the fan and about the unprotected pipe bends, which pose a real frost risk. I reveal my safety rule with the heating pump on level one in frost conditions. Eighth. The winter reality check and the roof. I show you the roof I built for my heat pump and explain why that's important in snow. I also show you in a photo the dirt from just one year on the fins. You learn why cleaning in autumn is mandatory and why the cooling fins freeze starting at plus six degrees because of the air humidity. Ninth. My honest assessment in summer and winter. I tell you how the eight-hundred-litre water tank is heated and the heat lasts through the whole night. But I also tell you the truth about rainy summer days and why the solar system brings almost nothing in the four hard winter months of November, December, January and February. You learn why my proven wood stove still has to do the main work in winter. This video is an absolutely honest experience report from a DIYer for DIYers. If you like my DIY project, feel free to write your questions in the comments.

evidence.text_en:
Hi [name],

I can well understand your experience. I'm a real estate agent and see this problem frequently in old buildings. 60°C flow temperature is definitely too high for efficient heat pump use. Optimal would be 35-45°C.

The problem usually lies in the insufficient heating surface of the old radiators. They are designed for high flow temperatures, but heat pumps work best with low temperatures. You have two sensible options:

1. Larger/additional radiators - relatively inexpensive effort, immediately feasible
2. Surface heating (floor/wall) – more expensive but the best long-term solution

For old buildings I would start with larger radiators first. Look for low-temperature radiators with more heating surface. That often already brings significant improvement without a major construction site.

Hello everyone,

we had an air-to-water heat pump installed in our 1962 old building last autumn. The first winter is over and I'm honestly a bit disappointed. The installation company said back then that our old cast iron radiators would work with the heat pump, but I have the feeling that the system is not harmonizing properly.

On the cold days in February we had to turn the flow temperature up to almost 60°C just to get it warm at all. That can't be efficient, can it? The radiators do get warm, but somehow different than before with the gas heating. Takes much longer and the rooms don't get really cosy warm.

Now that summer is here, I'm thinking about alternatives. Should we replace the old radiators with larger ones? Or maybe even retrofit underfloor heating? Although that would certainly be a huge effort in our old building.

Has anyone had similar experiences? How did you solve the problem? I'm grateful for any tips before the next winter comes.

Best regards
[name]

Hello [name],

oh wow, I know that! We had similar problems with our heating after our bathroom renovation. For us, replacing three large radiators on the ground floor already brought a lot of improvement.

A tip: Look for convectors or plate radiators with many fins. They have more surface area and get really warm even at lower temperatures. Our heating installer said that often just 20-30% more heating surface is enough to lower the flow temperature by 10-15°C.

Underfloor heating would of course be ideal, but the effort... For us, we would have had to rip out all the floors. Now in summer would be the right time for it, if you decide to go for it anyway.

as the others have already said, the problem is with the radiators that are too small. This is a typical issue in old building renovations.

evidence.text_en:
Energy Update August: AIRA Heat Pump shows 5.0 – recalculated it's X.X

**Small note on the dryer:** There was a misunderstanding on my part in the video. My wife didn't clean the normal lint filter, but the heat exchanger fins in the dryer. That also explains the significant difference in consumption!

Two weeks of vacation are the cleanest measurement a house gives. No cooking, no showering, no lights – and yet 13 kilowatt-hours per day. That's 41% of what an occupied house draws. You'll find all the numbers and facts in the article too: https://familie-elektrisiert.de/energie-update-august-2026/

August was a month with two faces: 1,202 kWh from the roof across all systems, 65% autonomy on the days we were there – and three dark days after vacation, when both cars were empty and the sun wasn't playing along. At the end of the day, 38 € electricity costs.

Two things really occupied me this month. First: My heat pump shows an efficiency of 5.0 in the app. When I recalculate, I get 3.7 – because apparently whole operating modes fall out of the manufacturer's calculation, yet their electricity still runs through my meter. I asked about it and will get back to you once an answer comes.

Secondly: A viewer had doubted my dryer consumption. He was right – just not for the reason he suspected. My wife cleaned the lint filter properly once. The result is more significant than I expected.

And then there are the 550 watts base load, of which I can't explain almost 500. Those annoy me more than the electricity bill.

evidence.text_en:
Hi Rolf,

60°C flow forward at a heat pump is really counterproductive. As immobilien_max already writes, that's way too high. I had similar experiences with efficiency with my air conditioning in the home office – [I also had problems with the correct dimensioning there](https://hausbesitzer-forum.de/community/erfahrungen-von-hausbesitzern/klimaanlage-im-home-office-split-geraet-oder-mobile-loesung-1780646441/).

For old buildings, hydraulic optimization is often the first step. Let a specialist check the hydraulic balancing. Often the volume flows are not set correctly. Additionally, you can equip the critical rooms with larger radiators.

Underfloor heating retrofitted is feasible in old buildings, but complex. Alternative: Wall heating or thin-layer underfloor heating systems. But first I would optimize the existing radiators.

evidence.text_en: Baffled and angry: I frequently receive heat pump quotes for review and often think: "wow, how can someone send that out." My findings: - Customers are sometimes really sold for a fool - Positions missing, subsidies endangered --> recently experienced again, KfW makes no exceptions! The subsidy conditions must be met. - Heat pump incorrectly dimensioned (way too expensive hardware, high operating costs through heating rod, wear through short-cycling) - Offers are outrageously overpriced. Due to the recent change in subsidies, the topic has become even more complex again.
